newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Ex-mutineers killed in Central African Republic.
newsitem.headline: Ex-mutineers killed in Central African Republic.

text.p: Three soldiers who took part in mutinies in the Central African Republic have been killed by security forces, a government statement said on Saturday.
The statement from the Permanent Military Court said the three had been killed on Friday night and a fourth soldier wounded by units of the paramilitary police.
No indication was given as to how the three former mutineers had been killed or whether there was any exchange of fire.

But independent sources said the three had already been disarmed after going to the police to demand the release of one of their comrades being held for the killing of an army sergeant from a loyalist unit.

In parts of the capital, shops were closed on Saturday in fear the deaths would trigger reprisals from other disaffected soldiers who have not yet responded to a government invitation to return to barracks.

The government last month invited all mutineers to go back to their camps after three mutinies in under a year and urged loyalist soldiers to welcome them back. African peacekeepers were asked to accompany the mutineers back to their respective barracks by May 16.

A first group of several hundred former mutineers returned to Kassai Barracks in the capital Bangui on April 18 under a new commander as part of a process of national reconciliation brokered by Mali's former military leader Amadou Toumani Toure.

Around 100 of the 700 mutineers remain in Bangui's southern Petevo suburb, one of their strongholds during the revolts, which began over pay and conditions but turned into a campaign to oust President Ange-Felix Patasse, a northern civilian who won election in 1993.

The first mutinies were in April and May 1996. The third, which began on November 15, degenerated into ethnic bloodshed. French troops, in the country under a defence pact, restored order and handed over to African peacekeepers.

Toumani Toure brokered a January 25 peace plan after clashes between mutineers and French troops but mutual suspicion between the mutineers and Patasse loyalists persisted. Mutineers and peacekeepers clashed in March.
The peacekeepers include soldiers from Burkina Faso, Chad, Gabon, Mali, Senegal and Togo.
The mutineers are principally from the southern Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba. Estimates of the number of people killed in the mutinies range from scores to several hundred.
